analysis_steps.goal: Grid the ejecta region, determine noise threshold, and extract integrated line profiles

method.value: Select a 0.6" x 0.6" region covering the ejecta (excluding the equatorial ring) and divide it into a 10x10 grid of 0.06" x 0.06" cells. Estimate the noise threshold by taking four regions outside the equatorial ring, dividing each into 10x10 cells, computing the mean absolute deviation (MAD) in each cell, and taking the mean of all MAD values. Mask out data below this threshold and integrate the spectrum over all spatial cells.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive observational fractional mass-velocity distributions and summary velocity parameters

findings_qualitative.value: Comparison of two epochs of SiO observations shows no significant time evolution in the 3D structure and mass-velocity distributions, confirming homologous (free) expansion and optically thin emission.

evidence.quote: In summary, the agreement between the mass distributions and 3D structures at both epochs supports the assumption that the ejecta are freely expanding, and additionally provides evidence that they are optically thin.

findings_qualitative.value: At a threshold of twice the noise level, CO exhibits a clumpy two-punctured shell morphology oriented nearly perpendicular (84 +/- 11 deg) to the equatorial ring, while SiO is dominated by a single large clump lying in a void of the CO shell.

evidence.loc: Comparison of SiO and CO morphologies
evidence.quote: We find a clumpy, shell-like structure that appears disrupted in two opposite facing directions for CO (red).

evidence.loc: Comparison of SiO and CO morphologies
evidence.quote: With the new threshold, the SiO morphology (blue) is dominated by one large clump, which lies in one of the voids between major clumps forming the CO shell.

findings_qualitative.value: Binary-merger blue supergiant (bBSG) models (particularly M15-7b-2, M15-7b-3, and M15-7b-4) best reproduce both the observed CO velocity distribution and the 3D punctured-shell morphology, whereas all bBSG models underpredict high-velocity SiO.

evidence.quote: The models which best match the mass distributions correspond to explosions of binary-merger blue supergiant progenitors; at least two such models approximately reproduce the observed CO morphology.
In contrast, the SiO velocity distribution and morphology are not as well reproduced in these models, indicating insufficient mixing of Si into the outer layers already at the progenitor stage.

findings_qualitative.value: In 3D explosion models, fast-moving Fe-rich plumes puncture and displace the overlying C+O shell, causing the densest C+O clumps to be anti-aligned with the Fe plumes and strongly correlated with the neutron-star kick direction.

evidence.quote: As a result, the densest C+O regions tend to lie in directions where the Fe-rich plumes do not penetrate, leading to the observed anti-correlation between the Fe-rich plumes and the densest C+O clumps.

Since the kick and the densest ejecta rich in lighter elements are expected to be anti-aligned with the most extended Fe-rich structures, a correlation between the directions of the NS kick and densest C+O ejecta seems natural.

claims.hypothesis: The molecular ejecta of SN 1987A are expanding homologously (freely) and are optically thin at millimeter wavelengths between 10,000 and 11,854 days post-explosion.
claims.experiment: Reconstruct 3D spatial maps and fractional mass-velocity distributions of SiO J=5-4 and J=6-5 across two ALMA epochs separated by 2–4 years (volume increase by factors of 1.40 and 1.64) and compare them.
claims.result: The 3D morphologies and fractional mass-velocity distributions between Epoch 1 and Epoch 2 agree within the estimated uncertainties (SiO average v_peak = 1600 +/- 110 km s^-1, v_max = 3560 +/- 50 km s^-1).
claims.finding: The ejecta are in homologous free expansion and were already optically thin prior to Epoch 1.

evidence.quote: The evolution between these two epochs is consistent with homologous expansion.

In summary, the agreement between the mass distributions and 3D structures at both epochs supports the assumption that the ejecta are freely expanding, and additionally provides evidence that they are optically thin.

claims.hypothesis: 3D neutrino-driven explosion simulations of binary-merger blue supergiant (bBSG) progenitors can reproduce the observed 3D morphology and velocity distributions of both CO and SiO in SN 1987A.
claims.experiment: Compare ALMA-derived CO and SiO fractional mass-velocity curves and 3D maps against C+O and Si+O distributions from 15 PROMETHEUS-HOTB 3D hydrodynamical simulations spanning single-star BSGs, RSGs, and binary-merger BSGs.
claims.result: bBSG models (especially M15-7b-4 with v_peak = 1550 km s^-1, v_max = 3550 km s^-1) closely match the CO velocity tail and 3D two-punctured shell morphology, but severely underpredict Si+O peak and maximum velocities (M15-7b-4 Si+O v_peak = 1250 km s^-1, v_max = 2650 km s^-1 vs observed 3560 +/- 50 km s^-1).
claims.finding: bBSG models reproduce the CO distribution well, but fail to reproduce high-velocity SiO, indicating insufficient silicon in the outer layers of the progenitor models prior to explosion.

evidence.quote: The models which best match the mass distributions correspond to explosions of binary-merger blue supergiant progenitors; at least two such models approximately reproduce the observed CO morphology.
In contrast, the SiO velocity distribution and morphology are not as well reproduced in these models, indicating insufficient mixing of Si into the outer layers already at the progenitor stage.

claims.hypothesis: The direction of the neutron-star kick correlates with the centre of mass of the densest C+O ejecta, allowing an estimate of the compact remnant kick direction in SN 1987A from ALMA CO observations.
claims.experiment: Measure the angle between the NS kick vector and the centre of mass of the densest C+O ejecta across bBSG and RSG 3D explosion simulations, and compute the emission-weighted centre of CO in the ALMA 3D cube of SN 1987A.
claims.result: In asymmetric bBSG models, the angle between the NS kick and the densest 15% C+O centre of mass is alpha = 2–33 deg (R^2 = 0.65–0.86 across bBSG and RSG models). The observed CO emission centre lies at r = 1660 AU (Theta = 8.0 deg, phi = 48.1 deg).
claims.finding: There is a strong correlation between the densest C+O centre of mass and the NS kick direction; if applicable to SN 1987A, the compact object kick points towards the observer at ~45 deg to the north.

why_this_data.value: SN 1987A is young and freely expanding so its 3D molecular ejecta retain the imprint of early explosion dynamics; high-resolution (<100 mas) multi-epoch ALMA spectral cubes allow direct 3D spatial reconstruction via velocity-to-distance conversion.

evidence.quote: Unlike older SN remnants which have interacted with the interstellar and circumstellar material, the expanding ejecta retains the imprint of the dynamics during the early days after the supernova explosion
In particular, the free expansion allows radial velocities to be translated into the third spatial dimension with much greater confidence than in e.g. turbulent molecular clouds.

why_this_method.value: Comparing both 1D fractional mass-velocity distributions and 3D spatial maps across 15 long-time (~1 yr) 3D hydrodynamical simulations is necessary because models with similar 1D velocity distributions can have completely different 3D morphologies.

evidence.loc: 3D maps of C+O and Si+O of theoretical models
evidence.quote: Although velocity distributions enable quantitative comparisons between observed and simulated data, these 3D plots show that a similar mass distribution does not guarantee qualitatively similar 3D morphologies.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Single-star BSG (B15, N20) and RSG (L15, W15, WH12.5, SW19.8, SW20.8, SW27.3) progenitor models were tested and rejected as matches for SN 1987A because they either fail to match the velocity distribution or fail to match the 3D morphology and progenitor constraints.

evidence.quote: Model B15 does not closely reproduce the ALMA measured velocity distributions of molecules in SN 1987A

evidence.loc: 3D maps of C+O and Si+O of theoretical models
evidence.quote: From Fig.9, it appears that model SW20.8 represents best the mass fraction vs velocity distribution of SiO. However, when plotting the 3D morphology in Fig. 14, we note that the distribution of Si+O does not resemble the observed 3D morphology at all.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Condensation of gas-phase molecules into dust was tested via ALMA Band 7 continuum modeling as an explanation for the discrepancy between models and observations at <1000 km s^-1 and >3000 km s^-1, and rejected as insufficient.

evidence.quote: Where many of the theoretical models have problems matching the observed molecular distributions is at velocities of $<$1000 km s$^{-1}$, where a number of them predict more material than is observed, and at $>$3000 km s$^{-}$ where they predict less material than observed. Condensation of molecules into dust therefore does not help us to resolve these discrepancies.

limitations_admitted.value: SiO J=5-4 Epoch 2 cube is truncated at +2000 km s^-1 on the receding side due to insufficient spectral bandwidth.

evidence.quote: it can also be seen that the SiO 5–4 data from the second epoch of observations (green line, bottom panel) is truncated on the far side at a velocity of +2000 kms$^{-1}$, due to the bandwidth not being sufficient to cover the entire range of velocities.

limitations_admitted.value: High-velocity molecular emission in the ALMA cubes may be buried in noise or excluded by the spatial cut-off used to avoid contamination from the equatorial ring.

evidence.quote: Too high model predictions for the velocity could simply mean that the material is not detected, because it is either buried in the noise, or it is at such high velocities that the ejecta are excluded by the truncation of the data to avoid contamination from the ring of SN 1987A.

limitations_admitted.value: Explosion energy and energy deposition timescale are free parameters in the approximate ray-by-ray neutrino transport scheme, and 56Ni yields have uncertainties due to the electron fraction Ye.

evidence.quote: Our approximate approach of the neutrino transport allows us to choose the explosion energy (and the energy deposition time scale) as a free parameter, and it is not calculated self-consistently.

Since our model comes with uncertainties with respect to the total amount of radioactive $^{56}$Ni synthesized, the discrepancies of too low peak velocities can be cured (partially) by assuming a larger production of $^{56}$Ni.

limitations_admitted.value: Simulations do not include self-consistent chemical networks for molecule formation/destruction or dust condensation, relying instead on local elemental stoichiometry (C+O first, then Si+O).

evidence.quote: The simulations do not yet offer the possibility to calculate the formation of molecules self-consistently. We approximated the molecule distribution as described in Section 3.

limitations_admitted.value: Converting observed line intensities into fractional masses assumes optical thinness, LTE, and uniform temperature across the ejecta without full radiative transfer.

evidence.quote: However, in particular, the assumption of LTE and constant temperature may not apply perfectly in the central regions of the ejecta.

limitations_admitted.value: Progenitor and explosion models do not include initial stellar rotation or magnetic fields.

evidence.quote: In particular, our simulations were performed without initial rotation and without magnetic fields.

referee_caveats_inferred: In the model stoichiometry, carbon is assumed to consume 100% of available local oxygen before any SiO can form, which could artificially suppress simulated Si+O in C-rich zones.
The 3D orientation of the hydrodynamic simulation grids relative to the sky was chosen manually by visual inspection rather than through an objective 3D cross-correlation metric.
In Table 1, rest frequencies are labelled in [Hz] in the column header but printed numerically in GHz (e.g. 230.54).
For the 2019 SiO J=6-5 dataset, the text states a beam of 115x108 mas^2 at PA 61 deg whereas Table 1 lists 0.106x0.101 arcsec at PA 70 deg.
